subject: chemistry-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: When magnesium reacts with oxygen, each magnesium atom:
choices: Gains two electrons to form Mg²⁻
Shares two electrons with an oxygen atom
Loses one electron to form Mg⁺
Loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺
items.note: Group 2 metals lose their two outer electrons to reach a noble gas configuration; oxygen gains two to form O²⁻.

items.stem: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
choices: Al₃(SO₄)₂
AlSO₄
Al₂(SO₄)₃
Al₂S₃
items.note: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: the charges balance with 2 × (+3) = 3 × (−2). Al₂S₃ is aluminium sulfide (S²⁻).

items.stem: An ionic bond is best described as:
choices: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms
Attraction between metal cations and delocalised electrons
Attraction between the nucleus and its own electrons
items.note: Ionic bonding is non-directional electrostatic attraction in a lattice. Shared pairs = covalent; delocalised electrons = metallic.

items.stem: What is the formula of the ammonium phosphate compound formed from NH₄⁺ and PO₄³⁻?
choices: NH₄PO₄
(NH₄)₃PO₄
NH₄(PO₄)₃
(NH₄)₂PO₄
items.note: Three +1 ions balance one −3 ion. Brackets are needed around polyatomic ions when there is more than one.

items.stem: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does because:
choices: In the melt electrons are released from the chloride ions
In the solid the ions are held by covalent bonds
In the melt the ions are free to move and carry charge
In the solid there are no ions, only neutral atoms
items.note: The solid has ions fixed in a lattice; melting or dissolving frees the ions. The current is carried by ions, not electrons.

items.stem: Ionic solids are usually brittle because:
choices: The ions are held by weak intermolecular forces only
A force shifts layers so like-charged ions line up and repel
The electrons in the lattice cannot move when hit
The lattice contains gaps where cracks start easily
items.note: Displacing one layer by one ion brings ions of the same charge next to each other; the repulsion splits the crystal.

items.stem: Which compound would you expect to have the largest lattice enthalpy?
choices: MgO
NaCl
KBr
NaF
items.note: Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic radius. MgO has 2+ and 2− ions that are small, so the attraction is strongest.

items.stem: Which property is typical of most ionic compounds?
choices: Low boiling point
Conduct when solid
Soft and malleable
High melting point
items.note: Many strong electrostatic attractions in the lattice must be overcome, so melting points are high. Ionic solids do not conduct and are hard but brittle.

items.stem: The lattice enthalpy of NaF is larger than that of KCl. The best explanation is:
choices: NaF contains ions with larger charges than KCl does
Fluorine is more electronegative, so NaF is more covalent
Na⁺ and F⁻ are smaller, so the ions are closer and attract more strongly
K⁺ and Cl⁻ are smaller and so repel each other more
items.note: All four ions have charge 1; the difference is ionic radius. Smaller ions → shorter distance → stronger attraction → larger lattice enthalpy.

items.stem: Which statement explains why many ionic compounds dissolve in water but not in hexane?
choices: Polar water molecules attract and surround the ions, releasing energy
Water breaks the ionic bonds into neutral atoms of each element
Hexane molecules are too large to fit between the ions in the lattice
Ionic compounds react with water to form covalent molecules
items.note: The partial charges of water attract ions (hydration). Non-polar hexane cannot interact strongly with ions, so the lattice stays intact.

items.stem: Which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic compound?
choices: Carbon and oxygen
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Chlorine and bromine
Caesium and fluorine
items.note: A large electronegativity difference (Cs 0.8, F 4.0) favours ionic bonding. The other pairs are non-metals with small differences.

items.stem: Describe the structure of solid sodium chloride.
markscheme: of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (1)
each ion surrounded by six oppositely charged ions (1)
held by strong electrostatic attraction in all directions (1)
items.tactic: Describe a structure: type (giant lattice), the particles, the arrangement, the force.

items.stem: Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
markscheme: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have larger charges than Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (1)
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are smaller, so the ions are closer (1)
Stronger electrostatic attraction / higher lattice enthalpy, so more energy needed to separate ions (1)
items.tactic: Comparisons need "both… but…" and must refer to charge and size.

items.stem: Explain why an aqueous solution of copper(II) sulfate conducts electricity, and predict what is seen at each electrode during electrolysis with inert electrodes.
markscheme: Ions (Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻) are free to move in solution and carry the charge (1)
Cu²⁺ ions move to the negative electrode, where a pink/brown copper coating forms (1)
Bubbles of gas (oxygen) form at the positive electrode (1)
items.tactic: Link ion movement to charge flow; predictions need an observation, not just a product name.

items.stem:
Data response. Lattice enthalpies from the data booklet (kJ mol⁻¹): LiF 1049, NaF 930, KF 829, RbF 795; MgO 3791, CaO 3401.
(a) Describe the trend for the group 1 fluorides. (b) Explain this trend. (c) Explain why MgO has a lattice enthalpy over three times that of NaF, using the data.
markscheme: (a) Lattice enthalpy decreases from LiF to RbF (1049 to 795 kJ mol⁻¹) (1)
(b) Cation radius increases down the group, so the distance between ion centres increases and attraction is weaker (1)
(c) MgO ions have charges 2+ and 2− compared with 1+ and 1− (1)
Product of charges is four times larger (and ions are small), giving 3791 vs 930 kJ mol⁻¹ (1)
items.tactic: Data questions: quote the numbers with units when you describe a trend, then explain with charge and ionic radius.
